claims.arxiv2606_00570: Methods that write new knowledge into a large language model by changing its weights are a workable option for instruction-following and reasoning models, both for single facts and for complex events, and both for one update and for many applied in sequence. Workable means that, at the same editing workload, the average over edit reliability, generalisation, locality and portability is at least as high as the strongest alternative that stores the update outside the model, while accuracy on unrelated general and reasoning tasks stays at 100% or more of what the model scored before editing, that is no relative degradation at all. Both the single-update and the sequential setting have to hold, not just isolated updates.
claims.arxiv2606_00570_c1: A weight edit aimed at one fact spreads disproportionately into the directions of the model's representation space that carry the least variance, and the size of that spreading predicts how fast editing quality decays as edits accumulate. Spreading in a direction means a change that is large compared with that direction's own scale before editing. Supported only if the most affected directions sit among the lowest-variance ones, if a single edit already exceeds the native scale of some directions, and if the amount of spreading correlates negatively, at p below 0.05, with at least three of reliability, generalisation, locality and portability, for at least half of the weight-editing methods examined.

0.text: Build the measurements the geometric argument rests on. Setup: 100,000 prompts from a web corpus, with hidden states collected by forward hooks at the down-projection of each transformer block for three instruction and reasoning models, plus the feed-forward projections of the layers a meta-learning editor targets in an encoder-decoder model; take the singular value decomposition of each layer's centred hidden-state matrix. Result: the spectra are sharply unequal. For one 8B instruction model, layers 5 through 25 retain roughly 75-80% of their effective rank but layer 30 falls to 50% and layer 31 to 25%; smallest singular values run from 3e-6 to 3e-3 and condition numbers from 4e6 to 1e8, so the lowest directions are orders of magnitude smaller than the top ones.

1.text: Check the approximations the analysis needs. Setup: measure how far hidden states move in edited layers after a single edit across several weight-editing methods, then track whether the original principal directions stay put as a sequence of edits proceeds. Result: a single edit moves hidden states only slightly in many edited layers, which supports treating the pre-edit basis as a usable coordinate system; dominant directions stay stable early in a sequence while low-variance ones drift quickly, which the authors flag as a limit on the idealisation rather than a global claim.

2.text: Are edits amplified in the low-variance directions? Setup: run 1,000 sequential edits with one locate-then-edit method on an 8B instruction model; in a late layer, project the hidden-state change onto the original singular-vector basis and compute, per direction, the change divided by that direction's own pre-edit scale. Result: the largest ratios concentrate in directions with the smallest singular values, and a single edit can already push that ratio above 1 in many directions, meaning the edit exceeds what the direction natively carries.

3.text: Does amplification track the decay of editing quality? Setup: at each editing step, summarise the per-direction ratio by its median within each edited layer and average across edited layers, then correlate (Spearman) with reliability, generalisation, locality and portability. Result: for one locate-then-edit method, three of four are significantly negative (reliability -0.96 at p<0.001, locality -0.73 at p=0.026, portability -0.81 at p=0.008) with generalisation not significant; for a second, all four are significant at p<0.01 or better. For an external-parameter method only reliability is significant; for a null-space-constrained method none are, and two are positive. So the relationship holds for two of the four methods examined.

4.text: Fix how edited models are scored. Setup: generate autoregressively rather than scoring under teacher forcing, judge semantic agreement on all four editing dimensions with a large external model, and separately check locality with a token-level measure. Result: the token-level check reproduces the semantic locality results, so the automated scoring is not an artefact of the judge.

5.text: What happens to factual editing as updates accumulate? Setup: eleven methods, spanning locate-then-edit, meta-learning, extra-parameter and external-memory families, applied to an 8B instruction model on a relation-extraction editing benchmark, evaluated after 1, 10, 100 and all edits. Result: after one edit several weight-editing methods look strong on reliability (79-83) but already score in single digits on locality (6.5-13) and portability (9-13). After the full sequence, five of them collapse to zero on all four dimensions; the best weight-editing survivor holds 69.5/55.5/8.4/8.6. The external-memory baseline is roughly unchanged end to end (81/75/17.5/40 after one edit, 84/76/16/46 after all), and leads throughout.

6.text: Does the pattern hold across datasets, model families, sizes and longer sequences? Setup: repeat on two editing datasets with three 7-8B models, verify on a 13B and a 14B model, and sample edit counts more finely than 1/10/100/all. Result: when degradation sets in varies by method, but every weight-editing method declines over longer sequences, and the external-memory baseline leads in all conditions tested.

7.text: Is the decay just an artefact of which facts were chosen? Setup: split the edits into facts the model is confident about and facts it is not, and repeat the sequential evaluation on each. Result: the same declining trend appears in both subsets, so confidence in the edited fact does not explain it.

8.text: Does the same hold for a reasoning-oriented model? Setup: edit an 8B reasoning-distilled model on the same benchmark and take the plain average of the four dimensions. Result: in single editing the best weight-editing method averages 26.0 against 56.6 for external memory; after sequential editing six of eight weight-editing methods average at or near zero, the best reaches 24.2, and external memory reaches 60.2 (90/90/15.5/45.3 on the four dimensions against 46/35/8/7.6 for the strongest weight-editing method).

9.text: Do edited models keep their unrelated abilities? Setup: after 10 and 100 edits, evaluate mathematical reasoning benchmarks plus three general knowledge and reasoning benchmarks. Result: two locate-then-edit methods hold up initially, losing 2.74 and 8.37 points on average, then fall to near zero accuracy after 100 edits; a meta-learning method is at zero after 10. The null-space-constrained method stays close to the unedited model after 100 edits and occasionally improves, though its locality and portability remain below the external-memory baseline. So one weight-editing method does meet the no-degradation bar, while failing the first.

11.text: Does it extend from single facts to events? Setup: process an event-level editing dataset and edit three models, in both single and sequential settings, comparing the strongest weight-editing method directly with external memory. Result: most weight-editing methods are unsatisfactory even for one event edit and break down almost entirely in sequence; the null-space method degrades relative to its fact-editing performance; external memory scores higher on portability, locality and the reported average for both of the models directly compared.

13.text: Is the one surviving weight-editing method stable, or tuned into working? Setup: vary its hyperparameters and the target architecture and repeat its evaluation. Result: its performance shifts with both, so its advantage is not robust across configurations.
